I've been doing this wheat-maize rotation for over 30 years now, so I pretty much know what works on my land. Last year the wheat gave me about 480 kg per mu and the maize around 550, which is normal for our area in Quzhou. I'll stick close to what I did last year with small adjustments.

For the winter wheat on my 16.9 mu, I already planted in October with a good improved variety — Jimai type that my neighbors and I have used for years. It handles our winters and yields well. I used compound fertilizer 15-15-15 at planting, about 50 kg per mu as base. Now in spring I'll topdress with urea at jointing, maybe 20 kg per mu. Total nitrogen comes out to around 20 kg per mu. That's enough — too much and the wheat falls over before harvest, I learned that the hard way years ago. I'll irrigate at jointing and at grain filling, that's the two critical times. If spring is dry I may add one more before jointing. For pests, I'll spray once for aphids around heading, and mix in the fungicide for wheat scab — the weather has been wet some years and scab ruined my neighbor's crop in 2023.

For summer maize after wheat harvest in June, I plant directly into the wheat stubble — no-till, saves labor and diesel. I use Zhengdan or Denghai hybrid seed, whatever the dealer has fresh. I broadcast compound fertilizer at sowing and then side-dress urea at the big trumpet stage. Maize here needs less water than wheat because summer rains help, but I still irrigate once or twice if July-August turns dry. One spray for fall armyworm and corn borer — that pest has been worse the last few years so I don't skip it anymore.

My wife handles some of the field work and my son works in town, so I hire a combine for harvest both seasons. That's my biggest cash outlay besides fertilizer. I'd rather put a bit extra fertilizer than lose yield — fertilizer costs money but a bad harvest is much worse.
